questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the limit given below?

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+2y}
$$

- The limit evaluates to $\frac{1}{3}$ along the path $y={x}^{2}$
- The limit evaluates to $-1$ along the path $y=-{x}^{2}$
- The limit exists and is equal to $\frac{1}{3}$
questions.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+2y}=\frac{0}{{0}^{2}+2\cdot 0}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

- Statement I is true. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y={x}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y={x}^{2}}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+2y} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+2{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{3{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=-{x}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=-{x}^{2}}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+2y} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{-{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}+2(-{x}^{2})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{-{x}^{2}}{-{x}^{2}} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\frac{y}{{x}^{2}+2y}=\text{DNE}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
{lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{\sqrt{xy+2}-2}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-4}=\frac{\sqrt{2\cdot 1+2}-2}{{2}^{2}\cdot {1}^{2}-4}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the numerator: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{\sqrt{xy+2}-2}{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-4} & ={lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{(\sqrt{xy+2}-2)(\sqrt{xy+2}+2)}{({x}^{2}{y}^{2}-4)(\sqrt{xy+2}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{(\sqrt{xy+2})^{2}-4}{({x}^{2}{y}^{2}-4)(\sqrt{xy+2}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{xy-2}{(xy-2)(xy+2)(\sqrt{xy+2}+2)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{1}{(xy+2)(\sqrt{xy+2}+2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,1)}\frac{1}{(xy+2)(\sqrt{xy+2}+2)} & =\frac{1}{(2\cdot 1+2)(\sqrt{2\cdot 1+2}+2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot 4} \\  & =\frac{1}{16}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $\frac{1}{16}.$

questions.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{3}+{y}^{3}}=\frac{{0}^{2}\cdot 0}{{0}^{3}+{0}^{3}}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

Let's attempt to evaluate the limit approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths. 

- Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=x}\,\frac{{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{3}+{y}^{3}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}+{x}^{3}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the line $y=2x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=2x}\,\frac{{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{3}+{y}^{3}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}+8{x}^{3}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2}{9} \\  & =\frac{2}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{3}+{y}^{3}}=\text{DNE}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,0)}\frac{{y}^{3}-xy}{{x}^{3}y} & =\frac{{0}^{3}-2(0)}{{2}^{3}(0)} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,0)}\frac{{y}^{3}-xy}{{x}^{3}y} & ={lim}_{x\to (2,0)}\frac{y({y}^{2}-x)}{{x}^{3}y} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,0)}\frac{\cancel{y}({y}^{2}-x)}{{x}^{3}\cancel{y}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,0)}\frac{{y}^{2}-x}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it using direct substitution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,0)}\frac{{y}^{2}-x}{{x}^{3}} & =\frac{{0}^{2}-2}{{2}^{3}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{8} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $-\frac{1}{4}.$

questions.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,1,-1)}\frac{y+z}{\sqrt{x-y}-\sqrt{x+z}} & =\frac{1+(-1)}{\sqrt{2-1}-\sqrt{2+(-1)}} \\  & =\frac{1-1}{1-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

However, we can simplify the limit by first multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (2,1,-1)}\frac{y+z}{\sqrt{x-y}-\sqrt{x+z}} & ={lim}_{x\to (2,1,-1)}\frac{(y+z)(\sqrt{x-y}+\sqrt{x+z})}{(\sqrt{x-y}-\sqrt{x+z})(\sqrt{x-y}+\sqrt{x+z})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,1,-1)}\frac{(y+z)(\sqrt{x-y}+\sqrt{x+z})}{(x-y)-(x+z)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (2,1,-1)}\frac{(y+z)(\sqrt{x-y}+\sqrt{x+z})}{-(y+z)} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to (2,1,-1)}\frac{\cancel{(y+z)}(\sqrt{x-y}+\sqrt{x+z})}{\cancel{(y+z)}} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to (2,1,-1)}(\sqrt{x-y}+\sqrt{x+z})\end{aligned}
$$

Now that the limit has been simplified, we can evaluate it:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{lim}_{x\to (2,1,-1)}(\sqrt{x-y}+\sqrt{x+z}) & =-(\sqrt{2-1}+\sqrt{2+(-1)}) \\  & =-(1+1) \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the limit evaluates to $-2.$
